```python
# 1. Reproduce the bug deterministically first: write a minimal failing test case before changing any code, so you know exactly when it is fixed and when it regresses.
# 2. Read the full traceback bottom-up: the last frame shows where the exception was raised, while the frames above it reveal the call path that led there.
# 3. Insert breakpoint() (Python 3.7+) or run under pdb to step through execution, inspect live variables with p variable_name, and avoid guessing at state.
# 4. Log values at boundaries (function entry, exit, and before/after suspicious operations) with logging.debug and f-strings, not bare print, so you can filter and redirect output later.
# 5. Bisect the problem: comment out half the code path (or use git bisect on commits) to narrow the fault to a specific function or change in a few iterations.
# 6. Verify types and shapes at suspect points with isinstance(x, dict) or len(x) checks, since many bugs come from str vs bytes, int vs float, or None sneaking in.
# 7. Watch for mutable default arguments (def f(items=[]) shares one list across calls) and off-by-one errors in range/slice boundaries; both are classic silent bugs.
# 8. Add temporary assert statements for invariants (assert result is not None, assert 0 <= i < len(data)) so failures surface at the true origin instead of far downstream.
# 9. Strip the reproduction down: remove dependencies, hardcode inputs, and run in a fresh interpreter to rule out stale imports, cached bytecode, or environment differences.
# 10. Explain the code line-by-line out loud (rubber-duck debugging); the act of narrating logic often exposes the flawed assumption before you run anything again.
```
